newsitem.title: FRANCE: Chrysler says Euro market looks tough - paper.
newsitem.headline: Chrysler says Euro market looks tough - paper.

text.p: Chrysler vice chairman Robert Lutz said in an interview published on Tuesday that the outlook for some European carmakers was gloomy because of rising competition in Europe with the arrival of Asian carmakers.

"The future looks grim for some of the Europeans," Lutz told the French daily Le Figaro. "Assisted by a weaker yen, which is no accident but the result of a currency strategy, the Japanese are poised for the turn of the century with major strengths," he said. Voluntary quotas on Japanese car exports to Europe expire at the end of 1999.
"Alongside them, General Motors with Opel and Ford, with its European branch, are equally powerful," he said.
"In a competitive and slow-growing European market, only the manufacturers that reduce production and development costs while producing innovative and attractive products will survive," he said.
Lutz estimated overcapacity in the European market at close to two million vehicles.

He said the European industry must become more flexible and develop innovative products to compensate for the disadvantages of a mature and saturated market. In Europe, the future belongs to small city cars, namely mini versions of multi-purpose vehicles, he said.

Lutz said Chrysler did not have ambitions to restore the presence it had in Europe in the 1960s and 1970s before it sold most of its operations. "The European market isn't in a situation that would incite us to re-establish major production," he said.
Chrysler has an Austrian plant in Graz that produces Jeep Grand Cherokees and Voyagers and it sold just over 100,000 units in Europe last year. It aims to double sales after 2000.

Lutz said Chrysler was among the more profitable car companies in Europe. He said that while its margins are narrower in Europe than in the United States, return on capital invested is higher in Europe. But he said the group was concerned by the dollar's strength.

To cope with its rise, Chrysler plans to obtain more components from European suppliers and ship fewer over from the United States. "That will bring the rate of local content from 50 percent to 75 percent on average," he said.
"The dollar's rise is pushing us to double our efforts in the company to limit waste," he said.
